content: The inclusion criteria for the study required pregnant women who were seeking antenatal care and screened positive for hazardous or harmful alcohol use based on an alcohol survey. The exclusion criteria included the following: gestational age greater than 28 weeks (44%), no alcohol consumption in the six months prior to study participation (19%), miscarriage between survey completion and telephone interview (14%), intention to receive prenatal care elsewhere (7%), inability to speak English (3%), intended abortion or false pregnancy (3%), current substance abuse treatment (1%), and other reasons (9%). A total of 1165 women were screened, and 886 agreed to participate. Of these, 532 screened positive, and 250 met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. These 250 participants were randomized into two groups: 123 in the intervention group and 127 in the control group. Follow-up was completed for 247 participants, and all 250 were included in the analysis. The intervention involved a structured Brief Intervention (BI) that included the following components: reviewing the participant's general health and pregnancy progress, discussing lifestyle changes since pregnancy (e.g., work schedule, exercise, diet, smoking, and alcohol consumption), setting drinking goals during pregnancy and discussing the reasons for these goals, identifying situations where the participant might be tempted to drink, exploring alternatives to drinking in such situations, and summarizing the session by emphasizing key points (drinking goals, motivation, risk situations, and alternatives to alcohol). These points were documented in a take-home manual titled How to Prevent Alcohol-Related Problems. Participants were informed of the U.S. Surgeon General's recommendation for prenatal abstinence as the safest drinking goal. The intervention also included the Situational Confidence Questionnaire to assess the participant's confidence in managing drinking situations. Participants were asked to report any alcohol consumption, even a sip, during the Timeline Follow-Back interview. Drinking episodes were defined as starting with a drinking day and ending after seven consecutive days of abstinence. Maternal outcomes included alcohol consumption and the number of drinks per drinking day. Infant outcomes included birth weight and APGAR scores. The study was approved by the Human Subjects Committee of Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was funded by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) under grant R01 AA9670. In another study, 2927 participants were screened, and 802 screened positive. Of these, 399 were successfully contacted, and 304 were randomized (152 in the brief intervention group and 152 in the control group). The intervention group received a single-session brief intervention involving the participant and her partner, while the control group underwent screening and diagnostic interviews only. Maternal outcomes included alcohol consumption. The study was a cluster randomized controlled trial conducted in the United States, involving 34 obstetrical practices across 15 counties in Wisconsin. Recruitment occurred between 2001 and 2004, with follow-up interviews conducted postpartum. Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Wisconsin Health Sciences Human Subjects Committee and 11 additional committees. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was funded by NIH NIAAA grant R01 AA12522. In a Swedish study, 303 participants were randomized (147 in the intervention group and 156 in the control group). The intervention group underwent evaluation by a research midwife, independent of regular antenatal care, and provided blood samples for biomarker analysis. Screening methods included the Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB) and the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). Maternal outcomes were measured using AUDIT scores post-intervention. Ethics approval was obtained, and informed consent was provided by all participants. The study was funded by the County of Stockholm Research and Development Fund, the Swedish Government Social Ministry, and the Swedish Alcohol Monopoly Research Foundation. In a South African study, 179 participants were included in the analysis (97 in the intervention group and 82 in the control group). The intervention involved an initial one-hour assessment interview, including consent, a personal questionnaire, AUDIT, feedback on AUDIT results, a brief intervention with goal setting, and notes in a take-home alcohol booklet. Two follow-up interviews were conducted, each lasting 20 minutes, and included feedback on drinking behavior, goal setting, and reinforcement. The final follow-up interview before birth included a brief intervention, feedback on drinking behavior, and a second AUDIT. Incentives in the form of food parcels were provided to all participants. Maternal outcomes were measured using AUDIT scores post-intervention. Ethics approval was obtained, and informed consent was provided. The study was funded by the Western Cape Department of Social Development. In a U.S. study, 30 participants were randomized (15 in the intervention group and 15 in the control group). The intervention group received personalized feedback, discussed the pros and cons of drug use, and engaged in optional goal-setting. Maternal outcomes included drug use, service involvement, and motivation at follow-up. Ethics approval was obtained from Wayne State University Institutional Review Board. Verbal informed consent was obtained for screening, and written informed consent was obtained for the full study. The study was funded by grants DA00516 and DA14621 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse.
